title: AI code vs AI Art
author: Reasonable_Team_7297
selftext:
I know this topic has been controversial and sensitive with some people . But I just wanted to put this out there

But the whole argument of AI is "Empowering" people to make games without the technical skills and "Democratizing" game dev feels a bit lopsided when its dominantly vibe coding centered than AI generated art.

People are increasingly forgiving of vibe coded games but push back very hard on AI generated art used in games.

Sure vibe code is not visible immediately but majority of AI disclosure on platforms like steam is regarding code not art .

This might be controversial but from my view its the design and code that make up most of what a video game **is** and not just how it looks . We had pong , atari , commodore etc where game did not have any art comparable to other arts of the era like movies and paintings, yet they thrived.

I feel its kind of hypocritical especially when game code is one of the hardest part of game dev and needs years of experience too , people really worked hard to learn it and become competent in that discipline, and its also a very strong part of how a game feels to play.

I'm not generalizing and frankly don't speak for everyone as I don't know everyone.

But now artists and designers can easily vibe code games because art is subjective not functional, but seasoned coders can't really put out even well made games with AI assisted art because there is immense pushback from community including other artists.

This feels like the gaming and game dev community is ok with taking from programmers and giving it to artists but not the other way around.

Coz I'm pretty sure if AI art was also acceptable , some of veteran game dev coders would also be able to make some mind blowing games , but right now they are at a significant disadvantage.

P.S I'm aware of say the Big walk controversy with AI code but they still walked away relatively unscathed , they still have a very positive rating.

comments.author: AdminClown
comments.body: The issue is that low effort slop is more noticeable visually through the art than the code and that AI still is not good enough in the artistic front as it is in the coding one.

comments.author: Arkenhammer
comments.body: For commercial games it is the customers who decide what is important. Arguing with other game developers about what is fair will get you nowhere.

replies.author: jaegernut
replies.body: For the customer to decide what is important, does that mean that it is also important for devs to disclose AI usage regardless of where it was used? Otherwise, how can the customer make an informed descision then.

replies.author: Arkenhammer
replies.body: AI use for art is usually pretty obvious. Generally the customer decides based on the quality of the product and AI art in games is much easier to identify than AI code.

replies.author: J0rdian
replies.body:
AI is not directly how a player enjoys a game. Whether it has an AI tag or not won't change the games experience.

It's the same thing with say the political views of a game developer. I may not want to support the political views of specific game developers if I knew they had those views, and if there was a disclosure it would effect me buying a game maybe. But I also understand they are irrelevant to the actual product.

So yes and no. It's a weird situation where people would like to know but it has no real effect on the product.

replies.author: Mormacil
replies.body: Ethical considerations matter, slave free chocolate, blood diamonds, sex trade free porn, etc. They all impact the enjoyment just not directly.

comments.author: qualiadev
comments.body:
Yeah I made a post a couple weeks ago basically saying the same thing. I know my technical background does help to a certain extent working with LLMs, but if I was a better modeler or animator I could do some seriously cool shit. 

I think artists are shooting themselves in the foot if they aren’t taking advantage of the fact that no one will care if all their game code is AI. You could have a team of artists and writers without any programmers and I’m sure they could create something awesome

replies.body: Gross mischaracterization for the overwhelming majority of people who don't want to consume AI content. They think the slop commissioner is human, but they disagree that the human was the one who generated the content.

replies.author: itsloopyo
replies.body: Like how a camera does all the work, and the photographer has no creative input.

replies.author: Armano-Avalus
replies.body: People just don't like looking at generic slop. They have a similar attitude towards using stock assets in your game. By your logic they are also "bigoted" simply because they prefer something that isn't developered that way. Wanting your cake you ordered at a restaurant to not be made with store bought cake mix is also "bigoted". You can disagree with people's preferences but calling them "bigoted" I don't think is a fair assessment of their attitudes.

replies.author: TheVoyant
replies.body:
Prejudice takes a new form every 5-10 years. 

Ai, Immigration, Political Belief, Gender, Orientation, Race...

The haters are always wrong, dont waste time on em.

comments.author: tschilpi
comments.body:
interestingly, frontier labs have put billions of dollar to enable superhuman coding, math, and systems engineering capabilities, and it seems we have achieved this point.

however, in terms of art and design, AI is currently worse than a mediocre intern at a games company  
So the fact that there is such a loud outcry about the art but not about the code baffles me lol

AI art is absolute shit currently and it's probably not going to get much better, whereas you can easily replace multiple junior engineers nowadays under the direction of a good game programmer / systems engineer

comments.author: PossibilitySpace
comments.body:
I think there's an uncanny-valley effect happening. People are so alert for things that match 'ai projects' and so primed towards disgust or dismay that anything noticeable 'catches' in the mind and then that's all they can see.

It turns up in AI writing, AI art, AI design and probably AI music too. 

Part of doing AI properly is to make sure that the final product you make with it feels human, feels like you put your intent into it. That, I think, blunts the effect of it being AI.

comments.author: swaza79
comments.body: It's for compliance with the EU's AI act (Article 50) which became enforceable at the start of August this year.

replies.author: llothar
replies.body: Nah, this is not relevant here. It is about interacting with AI systems, not AI-created systems.

comments.author: TheVoyant
comments.body: Make a good game and people will play it. Never cower to angry mobs, just focus on you and what you can control.

comments.author: Laperen
comments.body:
>But the whole argument of AI is "Empowering" people to make games without the technical skills and "Democratizing" game dev feels a bit lopsided when its dominantly vibe coding centered than AI generated art.

I feel this "AI art VS AI code" debate is besides the point, and the "Democratizing" should be focused on more. People aren't being handed a vote, they are being handed a tool. You cannot treat a tool as a vote.

I'd be more concerned about the entire entertainment industry as a whole. AI is capable of creating stuff for 1 sole target audience, its user. People are almost certainly more happy and proud with what they perceive as their creation, or at least something tailor made to their specifications.

This means, no external product could possibly match up. If everyone is capable of creating or tailor making their own entertainment, all facets of the entertainment industry are bound to die off based on the current trajectory.

comments.author: VortexAssetStudio
comments.body: You nailed the biggest bottleneck right now. Most backlash against AI visuals doesn't actually come from the tool itself, it comes from devs slapping raw, inconsistent images with messy borders straight into their UI. When the art direction is cohesive, properly isolated, and actually looks production-ready, players focus on the gameplay instead of trying to spot how the assets were made
